chunks: "The benefits of integration are that things on the same die are close, so you get lower energy per bit, higher bandwidth, lower latency, smaller area and fewer parts and solder joints.
The costs show up in several places. First, yield. Defects land randomly on the wafer, so the bigger the die, the more likely it has one.
Yield falls roughly exponentially with area, and the number of dies per wafer falls too, so cost per good die rises faster than linearly.

Second, process compromise: you can't put DRAM, flash, high-voltage power stages and RF on the same leading-edge logic process without penalties, so you either give up performance on the odd blocks or don't integrate them.
Third, interference: digital switching noise couples through the supply and substrate into PLLs, ADCs and RF, so a sensitive analog block next to a big digital block gets harder to design.
Fourth, thermal: you concentrate heat in one place, which creates hot spots and raises leakage.
Fifth, complexity: verifying dozens of blocks, power modes and clock domains is hard, and a bug means a respin, and that's expensive and slow.

The modern answer is to integrate selectively with chiplets: split a big design into smaller dies, each in its best process, and connect them with advanced packaging, so you get yield and flexibility while keeping short, wide links."
